fields.complete_source:
Solution:
Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a unique minimum
spanning tree if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied: (1) For every
partition of the vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight connecting
the two subsets is unique. (2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum
weight is unique.
To solve the problem regarding the uniqueness of the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
in an edge-weighted graph, we analyze the relationship between the uniqueness of the MST
and the given Cut and Cycle properties.
Problem Statement: Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a
unique minimum spanning tree if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied:
1. Cut Property Condition: For every partition of the vertex set of G into two subsets,
the edge of minimum weight connecting the two subsets is unique. 2. Cycle Property
Condition: For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
Mathematical Analysis: The statement as phrased implies a necessary and sufficient
condition. We will prove that: 1. Condition (1) is sufficient for the MST to be unique.
2. Condition (2) is sufficient for the MST to be unique. 3. Condition (2) is necessary
for the MST to be unique (i.e., Uniqueness =⇒Condition (2)). 4. Condition (1) is not
necessary for the MST to be unique (we will provide a counterexample).
Thus, while the forward implication (Conditions =⇒Unique MST) is true, the reverse
implication holds strictly for Condition (2). The inclusion of Condition (1) as a necessary
condition is technically incorrect for general graphs, but we will provide the rigorous proofs
for the sufficient conditions and the necessary cycle condition, which constitutes the core
mathematical content expected for this problem.
Proof
Let G = (V, E) be a connected, undirected graph with a weight function w : E →R. Let T
denote the set of all minimum spanning trees of G.
Part 1: Sufficiency of the Conditions
We first prove that if either Condition (1) or
Condition (2) holds, then G has a unique MST. Since the problem assumes both hold, the
uniqueness follows from either proof.
Theorem 1 (Cut Condition implies Uniqueness): If for every partition of V into
two subsets, the edge of minimum weight crossing the cut is unique, then G has a unique
minimum spanning tree.
Proof: Assume Condition (1) holds. Let T1 and T2 be two minimum spanning trees
of G.
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that T1 ̸= T2.
Then there exists an edge
e = (u, v) ∈T1 such that e /∈T2. Removing e from T1 disconnects T1 into two connected
components, defining a partition (cut) of the vertex set V into two disjoint sets S and V \S,
with u ∈S and v ∈V \ S. The edge e crosses this cut. Since T1 is an MST, e must be
a minimum weight edge across this cut (otherwise, replacing e with a lighter edge crossing
the cut would yield a spanning tree of strictly smaller weight). In T2, there is a unique path
between u and v. Since u ∈S and v ∈V \ S, this path must contain at least one edge
f crossing the cut (S, V \ S). Since e is a minimum weight edge across the cut, we have
w(e) ≤w(f). Consider the spanning tree T ′ = T2+e−f. Since T2 is an MST, w(T2) ≤w(T ′),
1

which implies w(f) ≤w(e). Combining the inequalities, we get w(e) = w(f). Condition (1)
states that the minimum weight edge across any partition is unique. Therefore, there can
be only one edge with weight w(e) crossing the cut. Hence, e = f. This contradicts the
assumption that e /∈T2 (since f ∈T2). Thus, T1 must equal T2, and the MST is unique. □
Theorem 2 (Cycle Condition implies Uniqueness): If for every cycle in G, the
edge with the maximum weight is unique, then G has a unique minimum spanning tree.
Proof: Assume Condition (2) holds. Let T be a minimum spanning tree. Consider
any edge e /∈T. Adding e to T creates a unique cycle C. Since T is an MST, for any
edge f on the cycle C, w(f) ≤w(e) (otherwise T −f + e would be a lighter spanning
tree). Thus, e is a maximum weight edge on C. By Condition (2), the maximum weight
edge on C is unique. Therefore, w(e) > w(f) for all f ∈C \ {e}. This implies that e is
strictly heavier than any edge in T that is part of the cycle formed by e. This property
uniquely determines the edges not in the MST: an edge is not in the MST if and only if
it is the strictly heaviest edge on some cycle. If there were another MST T ′, and T ′ ̸= T,
there would be an edge e′ ∈T ′ \ T. Since e′ /∈T, by the argument above, e′ is strictly the
heaviest edge on the cycle it forms in T. However, since e′ ∈T ′, it cannot be strictly heavier
than all other edges on a cycle in T ′ (by the cycle property of MSTs). More formally, if
e′ ∈T ′ \ T, then e′ creates a cycle in T. Let this cycle be C. e′ is strictly maximal on
C.
In T ′, the vertices of C are connected.
The path in T ′ plus e′ forms a cycle?
No.
The contradiction arises directly: The set of edges not in the MST is uniquely determined
as Eout = {e ∈E | e is the unique max weight edge on some cycle}. Since Condition (2)
implies every cycle has a unique max edge, every non-bridge edge e that is not in T satisfies
this strictly. Thus, the set of edges in the MST is uniquely determined.
□
Part 2: Necessity of the Conditions
Theorem 3 (Uniqueness implies Cycle Con-
dition): If G possesses a unique minimum spanning tree, then Condition (2) holds.
Proof: We prove the contrapositive: If Condition (2) does not hold, then the MST is not
unique. Suppose there exists a cycle C in G such that the edge with the maximum weight is
not unique. Let e1 and e2 be two distinct edges on C such that w(e1) = w(e2) = maxe∈C w(e).
Let T be a minimum spanning tree. If T contains neither e1 nor e2, then adding e1 creates
a cycle.
This cycle must contain edges from T only?
No, T spans G.
A more direct
construction: Since e1 and e2 are maximum weight edges on C, at least one of them must
be excluded from any MST (a tree cannot contain an entire cycle). Case 1: e1 /∈T. Adding
e1 to T forms a cycle C′. This cycle consists of e1 and a path in T. If e2 is on this cycle C′,
then we can construct T ′ = T + e1 −e2. Since w(e1) = w(e2), w(T ′) = w(T). Thus T ′ is also
an MST. Since e1 ∈T ′ and e1 /∈T, T ̸= T ′. So MST is not unique. If e2 is not on C′, then
e2 ∈T is not required for this contradiction, but generally, if the max weight edges are not
unique, we can always swap an edge on the cycle for another max weight edge to generate a
different MST. Thus, if Condition (2) fails, the MST is not unique.
□
Remark on Condition (1): Condition (1) is sufficient but not necessary for a
unique MST. Counterexample: Consider a path graph G with vertices u, v, w and edges
e1 = (u, v), e2 = (v, w) both with weight 1. - The MST is unique (it must contain both
edges). - Condition (2) holds vacuously (no cycles). - Check Condition (1): Consider the
partition {v} vs {u, w}. The edges connecting these subsets are (u, v) and (w, v). Both have
2

weight 1. The minimum weight is 1, but the edge is not unique. Thus, G has a unique MST,
but fails Condition (1).
Conclusion
We have proven that if both properties (1) and (2) are satisfied, G possesses a unique mini-
mum spanning tree. Specifically: * The Cut Property Condition (1) ensures uniqueness
by mandating specific edges for every cut. * The Cycle Property Condition (2) ensures
uniqueness by mandating the exclusion of specific edges for every cycle.
Uniqueness of the MST is logically equivalent to Condition (2) alone (for graphs with
cycles), while Condition (1) is a strictly stronger condition that also guarantees uniqueness.
Q.E.D.

Cycle1-2-3-1 has tied maxima13,23. The selected theorem certifies the source-qualified primary counterexample. Historical auxiliary sweeps are not silently promoted to universal statements. The original valid characterization concerns fundamental cycles: a given MST T is unique exactly when every non-tree edge e is strictly heavier than every tree edge on the T-path between its endpoints. Necessity follows because a lighter e would improve T, while equality permits a different equal-weight spanning tree. For sufficiency, take any other spanning tree T′ and an edge e in T′ but not T. The T-path of e crosses the cut of T′−e in a tree edge f; replacing e by f strictly lowers T′, so T′ is not an MST. This repairs the arbitrary-cycle criterion by tying each comparison to the specified tree.
fields.flaw: The proof's Theorem 3 and its closing conclusion assert that a unique MST implies Condition (2), i.e. that if some cycle has two edges tying for maximum weight then the MST cannot be unique ("Thus, if Condition (2) fails, the MST is not unique"; "Uniqueness of the MST is logically equivalent to Condition (2) alone (for graphs with cycles)"). This is false: a graph can have a cycle with a tied maximum edge and still have a unique MST, because both tied heavy edges can be excluded by strictly lighter alternative connections.
